I did this moving from New Jersey to New Mexico, though I moved to the desert rather than the city. Housebound most of my life by chronic illness caused by NJ's notorious pollution, I was stuck living with elderly relatives because they were so utterly change-averse they had done no improvements to their home since it was built in the late 1930s. Thus it was free of the chemical-laden crap and unhealthy ventilation systems that almost all US homes are built with. Unfortunately, this also meant I could never cultivate the kind of home business I needed to live independently as, again, no such activity was tolerated by these change-averse old people. When the last of them died their will required the house to be immediately liquidated and the money dispersed among the family at large, leaving me with nowhere to go and no way to afford to build a new home to suit my needs. Where do you go when you need a 'clean' home and almost all the housing in the country is made out of toxic crap? The only place where clean housing is routinely built in the country is the desert southwest--where some people still build houses out of adobe, compressed earth block, and similar materials.

As luck would have it, a friend I had met online through the space advocacy community rented a cottage from a landlord who was a 'natural building' advocate. He built things himself and deliberately chose to use natural materials because he favored their look and feel. He had another cottage to rent in a fairly remote spot that was made of adobe, soil-cement, simple plaster, and natural timber with peeled logs and lattila ceilings. Quite proud of his handiwork, the landlord was more than willing to be interrogated by my friend about how the cottage was made, so I was able to determine if it would be safe for me to live in. My friend was also willing to teach me about the college textbook trade so I could start a home business right away to pay the rent. So I packed up the old car I inherited and drove alone from New Jersey to the desert south of Santa Fe. It took me several weeks to recover from the trip but the work was not too challenging and I was able to start making a modest living pretty quickly.

I've been here in the desert ever since, with the Internet and the coyotes for company. Unfortunately, now this is all in jeopardy because I was attacked by a litigation mill in Washington DC working for several publishing companies. They've been operating without oversight from their clients and for some years have been filing bogus lawsuits for millions of dollars against poor and disabled people in courts thousands of miles away so there is no way for them to fight back. Their aim seems to be just to exploit the court system and bilk their gullible corporate clients out of billable hours, regardless of the lives they ruin in the process or the damage to the public image of their own clients. Their case is so absurd they actually claimed my little cottage in the desert was an illicit fish packing plant, and the federal court judge in Massachusetts never questioned that! My small savings has been lost, my health damaged by two years of constant stress, my business is being ruined, and I may soon lose my home. My story got in the local newspapers and I'm hoping it spreads and sufficiently embarrasses these companies and the court before they railroad me to death. I'm not very hopeful, though. At the end of the day it's all about class. The one-percent doing as they please and protecting each other while the rest of us get thrown in the meat grinder.

I picked up and moved from SC to Berlin alone, having never been before, not knowing anyone, and speaking only very basic German. I had a rough idea of what I was going to do, but spent 3 months living in hostels and crashing on the couch of new acquaintances.

I also always wanted to move out of the US because I hated the politics there. (I feel like it's an oligarchy with the illusion of choice and that the average person has no chance to change anything.) I also wanted to move somewhere with a healthier work/life balance and just different attitudes in general.

I wasn't terrified until my first night in a hostel. Had a bit of a nervous breakdown, but talked myself step by step into taking a shower. After that I kept to the plan and kept forcing myself to go out and meet people. I built a social circle that lead to more things.

It was the most free and exciting time of my life. 2 years on now and I'm still so glad I did it. I'm enjoying life here in Europe with new friends, new experiences, and a cute girl, traveling to cool places I would have only dreamt about if I was still stuck in the US.
